title: Hide Artifacts: Ignore Process Interrupts
summary: Ignore Process Interrupts describes running commands in a way that survives the signals normally used to stop them. Operating systems deliver signals to control process behaviour, and a terminal session sends a hangup signal when it closes or the user logs off. Utilities such as nohup detach a command from that terminal and ignore the hangup, while interpreter options can suppress the error handling that would otherwise end a script. The effect is that malicious work keeps running through a logoff or a dropped network session. This is not persistence, because nothing restarts the process once it is genuinely terminated. Detection looks at process ancestry and parent terminal state, at detached or reparented processes, and at command lines carrying signal ignoring options that are unusual for the host.

beginner.definition: Programs receive small messages called signals. Some signals tell a program to stop. For example, when you log off, your programs receive a signal that ends them. Some commands can ignore those signals. An attacker uses this so their program keeps running after you log off.
beginner.whyItMatters: If a malicious program stops when the user logs off, the problem ends there. If it ignores that signal, it can keep running and keep talking to the attacker. The victim may log off and believe the machine is now safe. The work continues in the background with no window on screen. This is why quiet, long running processes are worth investigating.
howItWorks: An operating system sends signals to programs to tell them what to do.
One common signal is sent when a terminal session ends, for example at logoff.
A command called nohup runs a program so that it ignores that hangup signal.
The program is then detached from the terminal and continues running in the background.
Script interpreters also have options that ignore errors and keep a script going.
Defenders can send stop signals to a suspicious process, and these tricks resist that too.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building with a closing rule. At closing time the lights go out and everyone must leave. A cleaner props open a fire door and keeps working after the lights go out. The building manager checks the front desk log and sees that closing time passed normally. Nothing in the log mentions the cleaner, who is still inside the building. Ignoring process interrupts works that way. The normal shutdown signal arrives, but the hidden work refuses to hear it.
takeaways: Some signals stop programs, and some commands can ignore them on purpose.
A detached process can keep running long after a user logs off.
Remember that this is not persistence, because nothing restarts the process.

objectives: Explain what a signal is and how it controls a running process.
Describe how a command such as nohup lets a process ignore a hangup signal.
Explain why this behaviour can outlast the user session that started it.
State clearly why ignoring signals is not a persistence mechanism.
Identify process telemetry that shows detached or reparented processes.
